title: Patch undo heuristics and signal notes
body:
Quick personal notebook for thinking about when to do a minimal revert vs full rollback vs hotfix after a merge. Goal: concise signals + safe decision flow so we stop bikeshedding in incident windows.

Context:
- Created after two recent small changes caused medium-latency spikes in canary then prod (late Oct deploys). Wanted a lightweight decision matrix we can keep in PR comments.
- Intended audience: reviewers, on-call SREs, and whoever is triaging the post-merge alerts.

Observations I care about (ordered by how fast I want the outcome):
1) Customer-facing error spike (5xxs) tied to a single PR cause: high urgency.
2) Latency percentiles shift without increase in errors: medium urgency — could be resource regression or batching change.
3) Canary failure on a fresh rollout: high urgency if canary matches traffic slice.
4) Non-deterministic test flakes that correlate with PR changes: treat as medium/high depending on test surface.
5) Database schema mismatch or migration failures: high urgency.
6) Small cosmetic regression (UI text) reported: low urgency — schedule next patch unless there's cascading impact.

Signals checklist (tick these quickly when deciding):
- Does the alert start within 10 minutes of the deploy? (yes/no)
- Is the failing host pool pinned to the new revision? (yes/no)
- Are there increased errors only on a subset of regions? (list regions)
- Repro rate from curl/postman against revision X vs previous: (high/low)
- Can we toggle a feature flag to isolate the change? (yes/no)
- Has the change touched cold-start paths, batching, or KV cache logic? (yes/no)
- Are tests failing on main CI or only in prod? (where)

Decision heuristics (handy one-liners to paste in PR comments):
- If 5xx increase and repro is high on new revision -> revert the PR and open hotfix PR to reintroduce later with instrumented guardrails.
- If latency P95 up > 2x but error rate stable -> rollback if customer SLA impacted OR create a canary rollback (reduce traffic) while we triage.
- If failure only in one region and we can route around it -> route traffic away + investigate; avoid global revert unless escalation.
- If test flakes spike on CI tied to PR -> revert if tests are gating deploys; otherwise keep PR reverted locally and run an extended CI pass.
- If change is a config flip behind flag -> flip flag off (fastest), prefer over revert when possible.

Minimal-revert vs full rollback vs hotfix: quick reminders
- Minimal-revert: revert only the commit(s) responsible (fastest for small logical units). Use when change is isolated and revert is low-risk. Command: git revert -m 1 <merge-commit> (confirm history first).
- Full rollback: move service back to previous release tag/sha for entire service. Use when multiple PRs combined produced regression or when rollback is simpler than surgical reverts.
- Hotfix: keep the current revision but patch the offending behavior with a follow-up PR. Use when regression is understood, small, and safe to patch without losing feature state.

Command snippets I keep forgetting:
- Revert merge PR (mainline merge commit): git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> && git push origin HEAD:revert-<pr>-<short>
- Cherry-pick fix into release branch: git checkout release/<service>; git cherry-pick <commit>; git push && create PR
- Roll back to tag: deploy job with --image-tag <previous-tag> or terraform/helm rollback step in infra pipeline

Triage flow (5–15 minute hot path):
1) Owner/ONCALL: confirm signal and collect repro (start timer).
2) Check canary/output from tracing to identify span/regression point.
3) If obvious and reproducible -> decide revert/flag/rollback and act within 15m.
4) Notify #oncall and PR author with concise status + action (revert/rollback/patch).
5) If revert done -> run smoke tests, monitor for stabilization for 30m.
6) After stable -> create retrospective note in PR and open follow-up tasks (tests, instrumentation, guardrails).

Risk matrix (quick glance):
- Low risk revert: small single-file change, no migrations, limited downstream consumers. -> prefer revert.
- Medium risk revert: touches lib used by many services; revert might cause other integration regressions -> prefer rollback or hotfix with feature flag fallback.
- High risk revert: schema migrations, breaking API changes, or long-lived infra state -> hotfix with careful canary or rollback to last known good if impossible to patch quickly.

Post-merge follow-ups (what to add to the PR or the follow-up ticket):
- Add a small smoke test that exercises the regression scenario (unit/integration).
- Add telemetry: feature-flagged metrics tied to the changed code path (count, latency, error).
- Add a canary gate: require X minutes of canary before global rollout for future PRs that touch similar code paths.
- Update rollout docs if deployment procedure had gaps.

Testing checklist to reduce future revert likelihood:
- Local replay of production trace if patch touches runtime critical path.
- Run fairness/latency load profile in staging for 10–15 minutes with representative prompts.
- Add deterministic CI job that runs on PRs touching batching/cache logic (smaller test matrix but more frequent runs).

Open questions / TODOs:
- TODO: propose a tiny GitHub Action to auto-add this signal checklist to PRs that touch files matching regex (batching|cache|kv). (next: write a prototype)
- TODO: align with SRE on standard canary threshold numbers (current ones are inconsistent across services).
- Question: should we require transient feature flags for all changes touching hot paths? pros/cons doc needed.

Notes to self (less formal):
- Keep the language in PR comments prescriptive and short: revert/rollback/patch + reason + next step. Avoid long debates in incident chat.
- Try not to over-correct — sometimes latency shifts need more than reverting (e.g., kernel/infra issues).
- When in doubt, prefer observable safety (toggle/flag) over code surgery when possible.

Recent examples (reference):
- PR #5583: small batching tweak caused P95 spike in region-us-west1; we flipped flag then reverted PR on Monday. Outcome: revert + follow-up hotfix with additional metrics.

If useful, copy this into PR template under "post-merge rollback heuristic".
